eligibility_reason: Section 2.2 defines an actor agent that maintains a short-term memory state per turn, cleared at task end and encoded into a long-term memory store M managed by a separate memory agent; the critic agent generates procedural memory entries from observed outcomes, and these are later retrieved by the actor to condition future decisions (p. 4). Section 2.5 describes run-time writes (generation, merging, pruning) and retrieval of that store (pp. 6-7). This is an externalised store the agent itself writes and later reads across turns, meeting I1. Year 2026 (arXiv 2606.06787, p. 1) satisfies I2; text is English (I3); pages were retrievable (I4). No exclusion applies: the store is written by the agent at run time, not fixed (rules out E3) or exclusively parametric (rules out E2); it is not a hardware/cache paper (E1); not a survey (E4); memory is the entire claimed contribution, not incidental (E5); the system is an LLM-based multi-agent architecture (rules out E6); the paper runs to at least 16 pages with a full method and experiments section (rules out E7).

facets.justification: Abstract states the contribution is 'a unified and automatic memory framework that integrates semantic, episodic, and procedural memory in a bi-level design combining short-term and long-term stores' (p. 1). Figure 1 and Section 2.2 show a prompt-resident short-term store (stack-based context compaction, Section 2.4, p. 6) deliberately combined with a long-term store holding a 'Semantic Heap' and 'Episodic Stack' retrieved via dense embedding search (p. 4, p. 6). The bi-level combination itself, not either tier alone, is what the paper argues for.

Section 2.3's critic-agent tool ('generate procedural memory') requires a 'reflection' field: 'Think about what can be learned from the result of the action... what should the agent do under the same circumstances' (p. 14) — content not present in any single trajectory step, generated by comparing expected vs. actual outcome (p. 4). This is the mechanism the evaluation centers on (procedural-memory ablation vs. AWM/ReAct baselines, p. 7). Merge/prune of existing entries (edit_in_place) also occurs during long-term management (p. 6) but is a secondary, not the evaluated, transformation.

Section 2.5-3 gives a declared fusion rule for procedural memory: score = v_m * psi(c_t)^T * psi(c_m), combining a learned effectiveness/utility estimate v_m with dense context-similarity, and memories are retrieved greedily by top-n of that combined score (p. 6-7). Semantic and episodic memory use plain dense (similarity) retrieval (p. 6), so the paper explicitly combines a similarity signal with a separate learned-value re-ranking rule for its central retrieval mechanism.

Section 3 (p. 7) states the system is 'tested on a variety of task domains bundled by the implementation of AgentBoard environment' against baselines ReAct and AWM, reporting task completion and average progress. Despite language describing conditions that 'simulate real task-solving agent environments', this is a public benchmark comparison with no real users or deployed setting reported in the given pages — the conservative, benchmark-scored reading is validation.

Section 3 (p. 7): fixed task suite (AgentBoard, spanning embodied AI, text games, web research, tool calling), fixed system prompts, baselines (ReAct, AWM), and reported metrics (task completeness percentage, average progress p_i) in Table 1.

Abstract (p. 1) and Section 2.2 heading 'Framework' with Figure 1 (p. 4) describe the contribution as an architecture: a multi-agent system (actor, memory, critic agents) organizing a bi-level, multi-type (semantic/episodic/procedural) memory store — an organizing system rather than a single technique, tool release, or dataset.
